4.title: Fugues for Four Voices, without Stretto

claims.claim: All ten fugues follow the general plan of Group 2: exposition etc.; entries in related keys and episodes; final section
Group 4 shows more clearly than Group 2 that a fugue may keep a general plan yet differ widely in details of form
A certain stamp is given by order of voice entry; they vary even in the exposition the succession of subject-answer relationships
Countersubjects: four fugues have one, three have two, one has three, two have none
Wider range of keys in middle section (up to five related keys in one); increasing tendency in four-voice fugues to use I and V for middle entries
Harder to judge exactly where the middle section begins
Four-voice fugues do not always make the relative-key modulation their first after the exposition, unlike most three-voice fugues

5.title: Fugues for Four Voices, with Stretto

claims.claim: Bach often alters intervals in one voice of a stretto for euphony
Where possible each voice completes the subject, but the stretto effect survives incomplete voices
Unlike textbook advice that the last entry of a stretto be complete, Bach leaves the final voice incomplete, normally to lead to a better climax
Subject-answer / answer-subject is the commonest stretto relationship, but these eight fugues use every other interval as well

6.title: Fugues with Countersubjects Introduced after the Exposition

claims: Most fugues in Groups 1-5 have a countersubject, some two, one (I.12) three; some none; type always evident before end of exposition
The four fugues here each show a unique experiment with countersubjects

typology.description: no countersubject in exposition; one introduced later

claims: The four fugues enlarge the concept of variable form; two fugues may differ widely in form and both be excellent
